images.title: Longer boundary, smaller area
images.purpose: Show a pair of shapes where the one with the longer boundary covers fewer unit squares.
images.composition: A before/after style comparison: a compact square on the left and a thin zigzag strip on the right, same size unit squares.
images.exact_structure: Plain white background, the main figure large and centred with generous empty margins on all sides, thin dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills, nothing else in the frame. Left: a 4 by 4 square made of exactly 16 equal unit squares, light #0072B2 fill, its outer boundary traced with a thick #CC79A7 line. Right: exactly 9 unit squares of the same size joined edge to edge in one single strip that bends like a staircase (right, down, right, down, and so on: no 2 by 2 block anywhere, each square touching at most 2 others), light #E69F00 fill, its outer boundary traced with a thick #CC79A7 line. Under the square: 'Perimeter 16' and 'Area 16'. Under the zigzag: 'Perimeter 20' and 'Area 9'. No other marks.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
images.takeaway: The zigzag has the longer boundary (20 against 16) but the smaller area (9 against 16).
images.description: Show a pair of shapes where the one with the longer boundary covers fewer unit squares.
images.context: Concept T2.C3x; one image showing only the main idea.

image_decisions.why: The claim is visual by design: the child must see a long boundary around few squares beside a short boundary around many.
